newsitem.title: USA: Brady bill will be "NRA bill," U.S. gun group says.
newsitem.headline: Brady bill will be "NRA bill," U.S. gun group says.

text.p: The National Rifle Association claimed vindication Friday in a Supreme Court ruling against a key provision of the Brady gun-control law, saying it meant the Brady bill would soon be "the NRA bill."

On a 5-4 vote, the court struck down a provision in the law which required local sheriffs to conduct background checks on handgun buyers. The ruling did not affect a provision in the law requiring a five-day waiting period for purchases pending a background check or an instant check.

At a news conference, NRA leaders urged the Clinton administration to switch immediately to the "instant check" system scheduled to go into use in November 1998, which would supplant the five-day waiting period.
"I really do feel vindicated," NRA executive vice president Wayne LaPierre said. "After all is said and done, the wait, under every scenario, is going to disappear.
"What we're going to be left with, when all is said and done, is not the Brady bill but the NRA bill that we advocated from the very start."
For years, the NRA has supported an "instant check", a basic on-the-spot background check. It says 17 states already have this.
However the technology is not yet ready to implement a full federal instant check system. The law requires that to be available next year.

Friday's ruling did not address the issue of a five-day waiting period, which therefore still stands as part of the law. Twenty three states are now implementing a five-day waiting period while the other states have different systems, including the instant checks.

The powerful NRA, the largest group representing U.S. gun owners, supported the challenge of the Brady law by 10 local sheriffs. They successfully argued it was unconstitutional to order local police officers to conduct the checks.

LaPierre said a better approach to fighting crime would be more aggressive enforcement of criminal laws. Only seven people have been prosecuted under the Brady law despite frequent claims that it prevents thousands of criminals from getting guns, he said.

"The key is to put 'instant check' on line as fast as possible," LaPierre said, later adding, "It has simply been a lack of political will in the Clinton administration that this (instant check) system has not been up and running."
